newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan VP vows to make more overseas trips.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan VP vows to make more overseas trips.

text.p: Taiwanese Vice-President Lien Chan on Saturday vowed to increase Taiwan international profile by sending more high-level officials abroad to counter China's diplomatic embargo.

"In order to survive and develop ourselves, we must go out. All of us must go out to expand our relations," regardless of whether the nations maintain officials ties with Taiwan, Lien told a press conference upon his return from an 11-day overseas trip.
Lien said the biggest problem and challege Taiwan is facing is from China which has repeatedly done all it can to try to sabotage the island's international relations.
China, which views Taiwan as a rebel province, has waged a diplomatic war with China ever since the Nationalists fled to Taiwan after a civil war in 1949.
It has warned other countries against forging ties with the island, saying Taiwan has no rights to participate in international affairs.
Beijing has interpreted overseas trips by Taiwanese leaders as an attempt to promote Taiwan independence, which it says would lead to Chinese attack.
But Lien said most countries which recognize Beijing diplomatically are actually quite friendly to Taiwan despite repeated warnings from China.
"Everywhere we go and see, we feel deep friendship," Lien said.
He said he was accorded with proper treatment when he visited Ireland, where he was able to meet "leaders from various sectors,' and discuss "economic and trade cooperation."
Lien refused to identify the "leaders" he had met, nor give details for any cooperation plan with Ireland.
Lien's trip to Nicaragua earlier this month for the presidential inaguration there was followed by a visit to the Vatican, the only European state which recognizes Taipei instead of Beijing.
When news reports about Lien making a side trip to Ireland, China reacted strongly by condemning the Irish government for permitting such a visit.
Beijing also protested the United States for allowing Lien's stopovers at Miami en route to Nicaragua and later to the Vatican.
Showing its determination to punish Taiwan's small band of allies, China made a rare use of its U.N. Security Council veto this month to block plans to send peacekeepers to disarm Guatemalan rebels.
China also sent its vice premier Qian Qichen to France last week, followed by a visit to Africa, where Taiwanese foreign minister John Chang was visiting seven diplomatic allies.
